comments.text:
Dark humor is basically an instinctive defense mechanism for those of us who work in the medical field. I have one story that gave me the most uncontrollable laughing fit of my life.

I’m a veterinary nurse, and one night we got an emergency case: a dog had collided with another dog while playing and somehow managed to split his spleen into FOUR pieces. We operated on him for four hours and had to give him a massive blood transfusion because spleens bleed like crazy and he was hemorrhaging badly.

The surgery went well, and the next day I came in for my shift and the dog was eating, peeing, acting normal… everything seemed to be going perfectly. Then suddenly he went into cardiac arrest. We performed CPR, but there was nothing we could do.

When an animal dies, you have to place the body in a bag before putting it in a freezer until the funeral service comes to collect them. The problem? This dog was a giant breed and weighed around 60 kilos.

So one coworker and I were holding the upper half of the body, both crying, while two other coworkers grabbed the back half. Do you know what happens to a body after death? There’s no control over bodily functions anymore.

Can you guess what happened?

While we were trying to get him into the bag, a jet of diarrhea suddenly blasted out at full force, and the coworkers holding the back end… let’s just say they had to run away immediately.

We laughed so hard we literally collapsed onto the floor crying. Every time we tried to get back to work, we’d hear our coworkers gagging or complaining and we’d start laughing all over again. We physically could not stop.

In the end, we just called the funeral service and asked them to bag him instead, because it turned out the dog didn’t even fit in the freezer.

Rest in peace, Willow ❤️

The speculum slicing you up has happened to me! They had just switched to new, cheaper speculums which had sharp edges from (I think IIRC) the specific plastic molding process. The more expensive ones had those filed down. It was like multiple papercuts and one big slice, I was the unlucky first patient and yeah, they took those out of service IMMEDIATELY. When actually properly tested, they sliced through the doctor's gloves!

Trust me, you do NOT want to know what a bunch of papercuts inside your body feel like. It's been 15 years and I still have to check every time I have to have an exam 😖

comments.text: 15:36  The elderly doctor who took out my gallbladder (1996)  when I was 22 cut my big artery in my chest. They didn’t tell me when I woke up. They asked me for a AIDS test because a nurse got cut during my procedure. They just kept checking on me and had me stay the night. They sent me home the next day. He even called me to see how I was. I thought he was being a good doctor. That day I sneezed and had a lot of pain. I called him and he said go directly to the ER. When I got to the hospital they said my doctor called them and told them what he did and that he thought I was bleeding internally. They popped me into a machine and I had a hematoma the size of a softball. I was no longer bleeding. They told me the doctor said they had to tie off my cut vein. I had no clue any of that happened. Afterwards I couldn’t stand up straight for a week. They said it would either dissolve or I would need surgery to remove it. It dissolved. When I went in later to get my stitches removed his hands were shaking so bad. He was ripping out the stitches and I was bleeding. This guy needed to retire asap.

comments.text: I was once roommates in the ER with a diabetic who was facing amputation and it was one of the saddest things I’ve ever heard. She was in with mystery weakness and illness. The nurse was a literal angel, and decided to check her feet when she heard about the diabetes. The smell of the wound when the nurse took off her shoe is something I’ll never forget. I started praying for her to survive the second that smell hit my nose. I spent the next few hours trying to be as low maintenance as possible while they did bedside imaging, called her husband, and got her situated for surgery. As far as she was concerned, because she couldn’t feel it, it was just a little cut she got while traveling, not even worth mentioning. I talked to my sister who works in the medical field about it and she said it happens all the time. If one of your loved ones is diabetic, please keep an eye on them and their feet! You might think they are sensible people, but diabetics so easily get a blind spot. She had a responsible job and a good life and couldn’t understand that her foot was dying, because she couldn’t feel the pain.

comments.text: I worked at a podiatry office as a medical assistant. The number of times I had to see the inside anatomy of a foot...and SMELL rotting flesh. Absolutely wild. I understand neuropathy. I have it. But I don't know how people couldn't SMELL their own foot decaying. I watched a doctor assess an ulcer that had tunneled through the patient's foot and she was convinced she didn't need to go to the hospital. The doctor took a long swab and poked it in the ulcer on the sole of her foot and it came through the top of her foot...and she STILL wanted to go home to her cats instead of going to the hospital. 🤦🏻‍♀️ Please take care and pay attention to your feet, y'all! ESPECIALLY if you can't feel them. There's more people walking around missing toes or entire segments of their foot than you realize and it's terrifying how quickly it can get to that point. 😅
comments.author: @ashleylaurenmarie
